text:
2.1 Continuous-time transitions and process covariance
The transition matrix is \(\Phi_k = \exp(A\,\Delta t_k)\) with entries derived in the matrix exponential section below. For each branch \(b \in \{p, s\}\), the process covariance of \((x_b, I_b)\) over an interval of length \(\Delta t_k\) has the block form \(\begin{bmatrix} q^{b}_{xx} & q^{b}_{xI} \\ q^{b}_{xI} & q^{b}_{II} \end{bmatrix}\). Writing \(x = \kappa_b\,\Delta t_k\) and using \(\sigma_b^2 = 2\kappa_b V_b\), the entries are
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^{b}_{xx} &= V_b\left(1 - e^{-2x}\right), \\
q^{b}_{xI} &= \frac{V_b}{\kappa_b}\left(1 - e^{-x}\right)^2, \\
q^{b}_{II} &= \frac{V_b}{\kappa_b^2}\left(2x - 3 + 4e^{-x} - e^{-2x}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The covariance is block-diagonal across branches because the drives are independent. When \(x < 10^{-3}\), the exponential differences suffer catastrophic cancellation, and truncated Taylor expansions in \(\Delta t_k\) are used instead:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^{b}_{xx} &\approx 2\kappa_b V_b\left[\Delta t_k - \kappa_b \Delta t_k^2 + \tfrac{2}{3}\kappa_b^2 \Delta t_k^3\right], \\
q^{b}_{xI} &\approx 2\kappa_b V_b\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta t_k^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}\kappa_b \Delta t_k^3 + \tfrac{7}{24}\kappa_b^2 \Delta t_k^4\right], \\
q^{b}_{II} &\approx 2\kappa_b V_b\left[\tfrac{1}{3}\Delta t_k^3 - \tfrac{1}{4}\kappa_b \Delta t_k^4 + \tfrac{7}{60}\kappa_b^2 \Delta t_k^5\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
For the vagal branch, \(V_p = \lambda_P\) (constant within a recording).

title: Supplementary material
section: 2.2 Dual-filter recursion, Joseph update and phase reset
text:
2.2 Dual-filter recursion, Joseph update and phase reset
Two filters are run in parallel and share one covariance recursion and Kalman gain. The stochastic filter \(\tilde{X}^{(0)}\) treats the observation as \(y_k = 1\) (that is, \(\nu_0 = 0\)), and the deterministic filter \(\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}\) treats it as \(y_k = \Delta t_k\) (the unit-\(\nu_0\) response). Both start from zero, with initial covariance \(P_0 = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_P,\ 1,\ 0,\ 0)\), which is the stationary covariance of the drives and zero for the phase integrals. At each beat:

Prediction. \(\tilde{X}_{k|k-1} = \Phi_k \tilde{X}_{k-1|k-1}\) for both filters, and \(P_{k|k-1} = \Phi_k P_{k-1|k-1}\Phi_k^\top + Q_k\).
Innovation variance and gain. With the threshold-noise variance \(R_k = \lambda_R\,\mu_k\,\Delta t_k\), where \(\mu_k\) is the artifact multiplier defined below, \(S_k = H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R_k\) (floored at \(10^{-12}\)) and \(K_k = P_{k|k-1}H^\top / S_k\).
Innovations. \(v_k^{(0)} = 1 - H\tilde{X}^{(0)}_{k|k-1}\) and \(v_k^{(\nu)} = \Delta t_k - H\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}_{k|k-1}\).
Update. \(\tilde{X}_{k|k} = \tilde{X}_{k|k-1} + K_k v_k\) for each filter, and the Joseph form \[
P_{k|k} = (I - K_k H)\,P_{k|k-1}\,(I - K_k H)^\top + K_k R_k K_k^\top,
\] followed by symmetrization, \(P_{k|k} \leftarrow (P_{k|k} + P_{k|k}^\top)/2\).
Storage and phase reset. The posterior states and covariance are stored and the integral components (\(I_p\), \(I_s\)) of both state vectors and the corresponding rows and columns of \(P_{k|k}\) are set to zero, whereas \(x_p\), \(x_s\) and their covariances are propagated unchanged to the next interval.

The measurement-noise term \(R_k\) contains only the threshold-level jitter. The uncertainty in the integrated drives is carried by \(H P_{k|k-1} H^\top\) and enters \(S_k\) but not the Joseph noise term. \(R_k\) represents the timing jitter of the depolarization threshold and the timing error of the acquisition system. The Joseph form preserves symmetry and positive semidefiniteness of \(P_{k|k}\) under finite-precision arithmetic.
Artifact multiplier. Let \(J_k = \max\left(|\Delta t_k - \Delta t_{k-1}|/\Delta t_{k-1},\ |\Delta t_{k+1} - \Delta t_k|/\Delta t_k\right)\) be the largest relative change between adjacent intervals at beat \(k\) (one-sided at the ends of the series). The multiplier is \(\mu_k = \min\{1 + (J_k/\theta_J)^{p_J},\ 10^{10}\}\) with \(\theta_J = 0.25\) and \(p_J = 10\), and the inflated jitter variance is capped at \(10^{12}\). As \(\mu_k\) increases, \(K_k \to 0\) and the observation has a negligible effect on the states. The multiplier references both adjacent intervals and is therefore not strictly causal; it affects only the observation-noise weighting and not the dynamics of the latent drives. Beats with \(\mu_k \ge 100\) are excluded from \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) and the likelihood.

title: Supplementary material
section: 2.3 GLS profiling and reconstruction of the states
text:
2.3 GLS profiling and reconstruction of the states
Because \(\nu_0\) enters the observation linearly, the generalized least squares (GLS) estimate follows from the two innovation sequences,
\[
\hat{\nu}_0 = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N} v_k^{(0)} v_k^{(\nu)} / S_k}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} \left(v_k^{(\nu)}\right)^2 / S_k},
\]
where the artifact-inflated \(S_k\) down-weights aberrant beats. With baseline-corrected innovations \(v_k = v_k^{(0)} - \hat{\nu}_0 v_k^{(\nu)}\) and \(\mathcal{K} = \{k : \mu_k < 100\}\) (all beats if fewer than two satisfy this), the concentrated estimate of the global scale and the profiled log-likelihood are
\[
\hat{\sigma}^2_{sys} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{eff}}}\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}}\frac{v_k^2}{S_k}, \qquad
\mathcal{L}^* = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\ln S_k - \frac{n_{\mathrm{eff}}}{2}\ln\hat{\sigma}^2_{sys}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{eff}} = |\mathcal{K}|.
\]
If \(\hat{\nu}_0\) is not finite and positive, the implied RR would be undefined, and the fit is assigned \(\mathcal{L}^* = -\infty\).
The reconstructed (forward-filtered) states are \(\hat{X}_{k|k} = \tilde{X}^{(0)}_{k|k} - \hat{\nu}_0\,\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}_{k|k}\). The variances of the drives include the uncertainty in \(\hat{\nu}_0\), whose variance is \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}/D\) with \(D = \sum_k (v^{(\nu)}_k)^2/S_k\):
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{x}_{b,k}) = \hat{\sigma}^2_{sys}\left[P^{(bb)}_{k|k} + \frac{\left(\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}_{b,k|k}\right)^2}{D}\right], \quad b \in \{p, s\}.
\]
The filtered RR at beat \(k\) is \(\widehat{RR}_k = (1 + \hat{I}_{p,k} - \hat{I}_{s,k})/\hat{\nu}_0\) with variance \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\left(P^{(33)}_{k|k} + P^{(44)}_{k|k} - 2P^{(34)}_{k|k}\right)/\hat{\nu}_0^2\). Because these quantities use the update at beat \(k\), they are in-sample filtered values. The stated 95% intervals are conditional on the MAP kinetic parameters.

title: Supplementary material
text:
2.4 Spectral anchoring
The relative vagal variance \(\lambda_P = V_p/V_s\) is computed once per recording as follows.

Resampling. The instantaneous heart rate (Hz), \(1/\Delta t_k\), is interpolated onto a uniform 4 Hz grid with a monotone (Fritsch–Carlson) Hermite spline, which avoids overshoot between beats, and the mean is subtracted.
Global wavelet spectrum. A Morlet continuous wavelet transform is computed [R package biwavelet]. Power at each scale is masked outside the cone of influence and averaged over time to give the global spectrum \(G(f)\), and frequencies are sorted in ascending order.
Frequency weights. A logistic transition \(L(f) = \left[1 + \exp\{-s\,(f - f_c)\}\right]^{-1}\) with crossover \(f_c = 0.10\) Hz defines the weights \[
w_v(f) = \phi + (1 - \phi)\,L(f), \qquad w_s(f) = (1-\phi)\,\left(1 - L(f)\right),
\] with \(w_v + w_s = 1\), where \(\phi = 0.25\) is the floor fraction of the vagal weight at low frequencies. The steepness \(s = -\ln\{\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)\}/(f_u - f_c)\) is set so that \(1 - L(f_u) = \epsilon = 0.05\) at the LF/HF boundary \(f_u = 0.15\) Hz, which defines the “sympathetic leakage” into the high-frequency band.
Energy ratio. Energies are integrated by the trapezoidal rule over the log-spaced scales on \(0.04 \le f \le 0.40\) Hz, \[
E_v = \int w_v(f)\,G(f)\,df, \qquad E_s = \int w_s(f)\,G(f)\,df, \qquad \lambda_P = E_v/E_s .
\]

The unweighted low- and high-frequency band powers (LF: 0.04–0.15 Hz; HF: 0.15–0.40 Hz) and the mean heart rate are also stored as diagnostics and are not used in the fit.
The anchor rests on two assumptions that merit explicit statement. First, the spectral weights encode external evidence about the distribution of vagal and sympathetic modulation across frequency. Pharmacological blockade paradigms indicate that parasympathetic tone forms a persistent baseline contribution to resting LF power [1,2]; because the size of this contribution varies across individuals and conditions, the floor fraction is set to a deliberately conservative \(\phi\) = 0.25 (a quarter of the low-frequency weight is attributed to the vagal branch) and is varied between 0.10 and 0.50 in the sensitivity analyses. In addition, sympathetic oscillations peak heavily around the 0.10 Hz baroreflex resonance frequency (\(f_c\) = 0.10 Hz) [2]. Furthermore, due to the sluggish intracellular signaling kinetics of beta-adrenergic cascades, sympathetic transfer is structurally limited to a negligible leakage fraction of less than 5% (\(\epsilon\) = 0.05) above the standard 0.15 Hz high-frequency boundary [3–5]. Second, the OU drives have Lorentzian power spectra whose integral equals the stationary variance (Parseval relation), so that the ratio of partitioned energies in the observed heart-rate spectrum is taken as the ratio of latent stationary variances. This ignores differences in the transfer from latent drive to observed heart rate (for example, the low-pass effect of integration over each interval) and is therefore an approximation.

title: Supplementary material
text:
2.5 Priors, MAP objective and optimization
The parameters \(\theta = (\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3)\) are mapped to the physical scale by \(\kappa_s = e^{\theta_1}\), \(\kappa_p = \kappa_s + e^{\theta_2}\) and \(\lambda_R = e^{\theta_3}\), which ensures positivity and \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\) without bound constraints. The log-prior terms, defined up to additive constants, are as follows.
Time-scale priors. For \(b \in \{p, s\}\) with default central \(c\)-coverage interval \([\tau^{lo}_b, \tau^{hi}_b]\) (default \(c = 0.95\)),
\[
\ln p(\tau_b) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\ln\tau_b - \mu_b}{\varsigma_b}\right)^2, \quad
\mu_b = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln\tau^{lo}_b + \ln\tau^{hi}_b\right), \quad
\varsigma_b = \frac{\ln\tau^{hi}_b - \ln\tau^{lo}_b}{2\,z_{(1+c)/2}},
\] that is, a log-normal prior whose central interval is the stated range, with \(z_{(1+c)/2}\) the standard normal quantile.
Separation prior. With \(U = (\kappa_p - \kappa_s)/(\kappa_p + \kappa_s) \in (0, 1)\) and \(1 - U = 2\kappa_s/(\kappa_p + \kappa_s)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ln p(U) &= (\alpha - 1)\ln U + (\beta - 1)\ln(1 - U), \\
\alpha - 1 &= w\,U^*, \quad \beta - 1 = w\,(1 - U^*), \quad U^* = \frac{r - 1}{r + 1},
\end{aligned}
\] which is a Beta density with mode \(U^*\) corresponding to \(\kappa_p/\kappa_s = r\) and strength \(w\). The defaults are \(r = 20\) and \(w = 10\).
Timing-jitter prior. The equivalent RR timing jitter at the median interval \(\tilde{\Delta t}\) is \(s_{RR} = \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\,\lambda_R\,\tilde{\Delta t}}/\hat\nu_0\), and a log-normal prior is placed on it, constructed as above from the central interval \([0.5, 20]\) ms. The hyperparameters are fixed and independent of the data, but \(s_{RR}\) depends on the profiled quantities.
The objective minimized is
\[
\mathrm{Cost}(\theta) = -\left[\mathcal{L}^* + \ln p(\tau_s) + \ln p(\tau_p) + \ln p(U) + \ln p(s_{RR})\right],
\] and non-finite values are replaced by \(10^{12}\) so that the optimizer backs off. Optimization uses the BFGS algorithm (R optim, finite-difference gradients, at most 1000 iterations) in coordinates scaled by the spread of the priors, \(z_1 = (\ln\tau_p - \mu_p)/s_p\), \(z_2 = (\ln d - \ln d_0)/s_d\) with \(d = \ln(\tau_s/\tau_p) = \ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s) > 0\), \(d_0 = \mu_s - \mu_p\), \(s_d = \sqrt{s_p^2 + s_s^2}/d_0\), and \(z_3 = \ln\lambda_R\) (\(\mu\) and \(s\) are the parameters of the log-normal priors). The map keeps \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\) and changes only the geometry seen by the optimizer, not the objective. Three starts are run: (i) the default, with \(\kappa_s\) and \(\kappa_p\) at the inverse of the geometric centers of the time-scale priors (with \(\kappa_p - \kappa_s\) floored at 0.05 s\(^{-1}\)) and \(\lambda_{R,0} = 10^{-3}\); (ii) a noise-free start (\(\tau_p\) = 12 s, \(\tau_s\) = 160 s, \(\lambda_R = 10^{-6}\)); and (iii) a noisy start (\(\tau_p\) = 25 s, \(\tau_s\) = 150 s, \(\lambda_R = 0.3\)). The last two cover the two ends of the noise-to-signal ratio, which spans several orders of magnitude and where narrow secondary optima were found in preliminary checks with a single start. The run with the lowest cost is kept, and among runs within 0.01 of the lowest the earliest, because runs that reach the same optimum differ by the optimizer tolerance. The default start reached the lowest objective (within 0.01) in 306 of 313 recordings; in the other 7 (2%), 4 from the noise-free start and 3 from the noisy start, the lowest objective was below that of the default start by a median of 46.6 (range 10.2 to 662.7). Three starts do not guarantee a global optimum.

title: Supplementary material
text:
2.6 Parameter uncertainty
Standard errors are computed from the numerical Hessian \(\mathcal{H}\) of \(\mathrm{Cost}(\theta)\) at the optimum. The covariance of \(\theta\) is approximated by the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse \(\mathcal{H}^{+}\), which tolerates near-singularity, and mapped to the physical parameters through the Jacobian \(\mathcal{J}\) of \(\theta \mapsto (\kappa_s, \kappa_p, \lambda_R)\), giving \(\mathrm{Cov} = \mathcal{J}\,\mathcal{H}^{+}\,\mathcal{J}^\top\). For the time constants, the delta method gives \(\mathrm{Var}(\tau) \approx \mathrm{Var}(\kappa)/\kappa^4\). Wald 95% intervals are \(\text{estimate} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}\). The profiled (\(\hat\nu_0\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\)), fixed (\(\lambda_P\), hyperparameters) and derived quantities carry no standard error, and the intervals therefore do not reflect uncertainty in \(\lambda_P\) or in the hyperparameters.

title: Supplementary material
text:
3.1 The classical Poisson arrival formulation
In classical point-process statistics, a heartbeat is a stochastic arrival governed by a conditional intensity function \(\lambda(t)\). The time-rescaling theorem states that integrating the intensity over the observed inter-beat interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\),
\[
\Lambda_k = \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} \lambda(t)\, dt,
\]
transforms the sequence of intervals into unit-rate exponential variates, \(\Lambda_k \sim \text{Exp}(1)\). The exponential CDF maps these to a uniform distribution:
\[
u_k = 1 - \exp(-\Lambda_k) \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1),
\]
which is evaluated with the KS test.

title: Supplementary material
text:
3.2 The phase-domain diffusion formulation
In SPARK, the event is triggered when the accumulated phase reaches a threshold of \(1\), and the stochasticity arises from the diffusion within the interval together with uncertainty about the latent drives. Over the observed interval, the filter predicts the phase from the past data and the baseline, and the innovation is
\[
v_k = v_k^{(0)} - \hat{\nu}_0\,v_k^{(\nu)} = 1 - \hat{\nu}_0\,\Delta t_k - H\,\hat{X}_{k|k-1},
\]
the difference between the observed unit phase and its one-step-ahead prediction. If the model and the parameters are correct, \(v_k\) is conditionally Gaussian with zero mean and variance \(\sigma^2_{sys} S_k\), where \(S_k = H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R_k\) combines the prediction uncertainty of the integrated drives and the threshold noise. In contrast to the exponential variates of the Poisson formulation, the standardized innovation is therefore normal.

title: Supplementary material
section: 3.3 Standardization and the probability integral transform
text:
3.3 Standardization and the probability integral transform
The standardized innovation is
\[
z_k = \frac{v_k}{\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\,S_k}} \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
\]
and the probability integral transform with the standard normal CDF gives
\[
u_k = \Phi(z_k) \;\approx\; \mathcal{U}(0, 1).
\]
Uniformity of \(u_k\) is assessed with the KS distance \(D\), and the approximate 5% critical value is \(1.36/\sqrt{N}\). Because \(\hat{\nu}_0\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) and the kinetic parameters are estimated from the same series, the nominal critical value is approximate, and the test is conservative in this respect. Serial independence is assessed with the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) of \(z_k\) over 40 lags, with bounds at \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\). Diagnostics retain beats with finite innovations and artifact multiplier \(\mu_k < 1.5\), and the innovation variance used for standardization excludes the artifact inflation. The plug-in values used for \(\hat\nu_0\) and \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) make the standardized innovations approximate.
The diagnostic is the probability integral transform of the model-standardized innovations: \(u_k = \Phi(z_k)\) with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, and not \(1 - e^{-\Lambda_k}\) as in the time-rescaling theorem. It shares with time-rescaling the idea of isolating the model-standardized noise and mapping it to a uniform distribution, and it is not an application of the Poisson-specific theorem. Agreement with uniformity and serial independence is necessary for adequacy but does not establish it, since the diagnostics may have limited power against specific misspecifications, including the structure of the latent decomposition.

title: Supplementary material
section: 5.1 Explicit derivation of the transition matrix
text:
5.1 Explicit derivation of the transition matrix
The matrix exponential is evaluated from its Taylor series,
\[
\exp(A\,\Delta t_k) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(A\,\Delta t_k)^n}{n!} = I + A\,\Delta t_k + \frac{1}{2!} A^2 \Delta t_k^2 + \dots
\]
Given the block structure of \(A\), its powers follow a regular pattern. For any integer \(n \ge 1\),
\[
A^n = \begin{bmatrix}
(-\kappa_p)^n & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & (-\kappa_s)^n & 0 & 0 \\
(-\kappa_p)^{n-1} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & (-\kappa_s)^{n-1} & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For the top-left element, which governs \(x_p\), the series reduces to the scalar exponential:
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-\kappa_p \Delta t_k)^n}{n!} = e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k}.
\]
For the element in position \((3,1)\), which governs \(I_p\), the series starts at \(n = 1\), because the identity matrix has a zero in this position. Extracting a factor of \(-1/\kappa_p\) gives
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\Delta t_k^n}{n!} (-\kappa_p)^{n-1} = -\frac{1}{\kappa_p} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-\kappa_p \Delta t_k)^n}{n!}.
\]
The right-hand sum is the Taylor series of \(e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k}\) minus its \(n = 0\) term, which equals \(1\), so that
\[
-\frac{1}{\kappa_p} \left( e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k} - 1 \right) = \frac{1 - e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k}}{\kappa_p}.
\]
Because the vagal and sympathetic pathways are decoupled in \(A\), the same reduction applies to the sympathetic parameters. The element in position \((2,2)\) is
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-\kappa_s \Delta t_k)^n}{n!} = e^{-\kappa_s \Delta t_k},
\]
and the element in position \((4,2)\) is
\[
-\frac{1}{\kappa_s} \left( e^{-\kappa_s \Delta t_k} - 1 \right) = \frac{1 - e^{-\kappa_s \Delta t_k}}{\kappa_s}.
\]
Finally, the right half of \(A^n\) is zero for all \(n \ge 1\), so the elements in positions \((3,3)\) and \((4,4)\) come only from the identity matrix and equal \(1\). Assembling these scalar solutions gives the closed-form transition matrix \(\Phi_k\), in which the accumulation of the integral states is evaluated analytically and without numerical integration over each interval.

title: Supplementary material
text:
21.1 Path survival and artifact weighting
In the strict first-passage formulation the beat occurs the first time \(\phi\) touches the threshold, so \(\phi\) must stay below \(1\) during the whole interval. The terminal-threshold condition uses only the value of the phase at \(t_k\) and drops this path-survival requirement; it therefore neglects the paths that reach the threshold earlier within the interval and then fall back below it. This is accurate when the drift is large relative to the noise, because such paths are then rare (section “Asymptotic convergence”). To limit the influence of ectopic beats and detection artifacts, the threshold-noise variance at beat \(k\) is inflated by a multiplier that grows with the largest relative change between adjacent intervals, which removes abrupt jumps from the likelihood without interrupting the propagation of the drives. The multiplier uses both the preceding and the following interval and is therefore not strictly causal; it affects only the weighting of the observation. It is a heuristic robustness device and not a model of arrhythmia. The profiled log-likelihood is computed over the beats with a multiplier below 100, and the PACF diagnostic uses the beats with a multiplier below 1.5.

title: Supplementary material
text:
21.2 Justification of the identification structure
Structural constraints. Exponential links ensure positive rates, and \(\kappa_p = \kappa_s + \exp(\theta_2)\) imposes \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\), which removes label switching, that is, the interchangeability of the two drives (a solution in which the fast and the slow process exchange roles would otherwise fit the intervals equally well).
Time-scale information. Independent log-normal priors on \(\tau_p\) and \(\tau_s\), and a Beta prior on \(U\) that discourages the two time scales from collapsing onto one another, reflect the expected separation between rapid vagal and slow sympathetic effector kinetics [10,11]. The limits for \(\tau_p\) align with rapid parasympathetic signaling and respiratory cycles, and those for \(\tau_s\) with the inertia and low-pass behavior of sympathetic modulation [2,11,12]. The priors are fixed across recordings and not derived from the individual series.
Spectral information. The global wavelet spectrum of the heart rate [13,14] is partitioned into vagal and sympathetic energy with logistic frequency weights: sympathetic weight dominates at low frequencies, vagal weight rises at a crossover of 0.10 Hz, sympathetic weight falls to 5% at the boundary between the LF and HF bands at 0.15 Hz, and the vagal branch keeps a floor fraction of the low-frequency weight to reflect its contribution under non-stationarity. The weights encode external evidence on how modulation by the two branches is distributed across frequency, including pharmacological-blockade studies [1–4,15]. The physiological information resides in the weighting function; the ratio itself is computed from the series being fitted (section “Spectral anchoring”).
Timing jitter. The equivalent RR timing jitter is the SD, in milliseconds, of the error in the timing of each beat that the threshold-level noise produces; it is the noise term that could otherwise absorb autonomic variability. Its prior, with a 95% interval of 0.5–20 ms, spans the range expected for electrocardiographic and photoplethysmographic acquisition.

title: Supplementary material
text:
21.3 Inference, diagnostics and identifiability analyses
Optimization. The MAP objective is minimized by BFGS in coordinates scaled by the spread of the time-scale priors, started from the centers of the priors and from two points with negligible and with dominant observation noise; the run with the lowest objective is kept. Profiled, fixed and derived quantities carry no standard error.
Innovation diagnostics. The standardized innovations are \(z_k = v_k/\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{sys}S_k}\), where \(v_k\) is the one-step prediction error of the observation and \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}S_k\) its variance. The mapping \(u_k = \Phi(z_k)\) to uniformity is the same idea as in the time-rescaling diagnostics of point-process models, but it is not an application of the time-rescaling theorem: the innovations of SPARK are Gaussian, so the transform is \(\Phi\) and not \(1 - e^{-\Lambda}\) (section “Goodness-of-fit diagnostic”). The critical value \(1.36/\sqrt{N}\) is approximate because the parameters are estimated from the same data, so the distribution of \(D\) across recordings is reported instead of dichotomous \(p\)-value thresholds; the PACF bounds are \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\).
Identifiability analyses. Of the dispersed starting points, the first is the engine default and the others are drawn log-uniformly over wide ranges; the subset of recordings is balanced across groups in the Fantasia database. The specifications are alternative assemblies of the engine’s own likelihood and log-prior terms, and the compiled filter used inside the optimizer was verified against the engine’s filter (section “Identifiability and sensitivity analyses: details”). The numerical Hessian of the objective at the best fit of \(M_0\) and \(M_3\) was also decomposed.
Fitted time constants. The estimated clearance rates of \(M_3\) were 0.07 s\(^{-1}\) [0.02, 0.38] for the vagal drive, corresponding to an e-folding time of 15.05 s [2.61, 44.17], and 0.007 s\(^{-1}\) [0.005, 0.009] for the sympathetic drive, corresponding to 150.0 s [112.6, 220.9] (Figure S 10, panel D). They are MAP estimates under informative physiological priors and an enforced ordering \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\), so the separation of the two time scales does not by itself constitute independent evidence that the two drives have been segregated “blindly”; the extent to which the data move the estimates away from the prior centers is quantified by the contraction and prior-contrast values of the main text.

title: Supplementary material
text:
21.4 Events, perturbation and exercise
Events. For the recordings without tilt angle or annotations and for the exercise recordings, heart rate in 5-s bins was segmented into piecewise-constant levels, with the number of segments chosen by the Bayesian information criterion subject to a minimum difference of 0.10 Hz (about 6 bpm) between adjacent levels. Heart rate alone cannot tell a tilt from another maneuver that raises it, so such events are candidates, not confirmed tilts, and the analyses emphasize the relative timing and amplitude of the two components.
Orthostatic perturbation. Step-response fits at the search bounds are flagged. The share of individual tilts with the expected pattern is reported as a measure of within-recording consistency, alongside the between-recording summary in which each recording contributes the median over its tilts. Reconstructions are displayed as time series with 95% intervals, as averages of tilts aligned on the onset (each relative to its own baseline) and as trajectories in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in units of the baseline SDs.
Exercise geometry. The path summaries are not established statistics of HRV analysis: the length is the distance travelled in the state plane, the enclosed area is the extent of the region that the path encloses, and the maximum energy \(E\), half the squared distance from the homeostatic baseline, reflects the largest excursion from rest. No clinical or functional outcomes and no subject characteristics were available for this cohort, so no analyses of association with such variables were performed. The recovery-time benchmark depends on the simulated profiles and is a methodological check of the definitions, not evidence about the real recordings.

title: Supplementary material
text:
21.5 Extended discussion
Exact transitions. The transitions of the filter are the transition kernels of the latent drives from one observed beat to the next. Because the drives are Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, the distribution of the state at the next beat given the current one is Gaussian, with a mean and covariance known in closed form (the matrix exponential \(\Phi_k\) and its process covariance), so no Euler–Maruyama or other time-stepping approximation of the dynamics is needed, however irregular the intervals are. The bound on the neglected boundary term is small in the high-drift, low-noise regime but is not zero, and it should be examined in recordings with large threshold noise.
Interval-variance scaling. Under the strict first-passage formulation, the variance of the interval scales with the inverse cube of the drift, in qualitative agreement with the usual observation that respiratory sinus arrhythmia is larger when vagal influence is high, although its amplitude is not a pure index of vagal tone (section “Interval-variance scaling”). SPARK conditions on the observed interval and uses a Gaussian measurement equation whose variance does not depend on the vagal level, so this dependence is not represented, and the stationary variances of the two drives are treated as constant within a recording.
Relation to nonlinear stochastic dynamics. Seen as a dynamical system, SPARK couples a fast and a slow mean-reverting stochastic process to a threshold-crossing phase oscillator that is reset at every event, and the data are the crossing times. The observation is a first-passage problem, which the terminal-threshold condition makes tractable by exact linear-Gaussian filtering; the continuous-time drives evolve without interruption, and only the integral states, which accumulate phase, are reset at each beat, so the system mixes continuous dynamics with discrete events. Identifiability is then a question about time-scale separation: the fitted rates of the two drives differ by a median factor of 10 in these recordings, and when the likelihood is left unconstrained it shows ridges along which solutions with very different time scales and variance partitions fit the intervals almost equally well (section 3.1 of the main text); external information on the time scales and on how variance is distributed across frequency removes this degeneracy (neither source alone does; Table 3 of the main text), and it does so by assumption and not by the data. Because the filter keeps the continuous-time trajectories of both drives, the response of a perturbed system relaxing towards its baseline can be described geometrically in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane; these are descriptive summaries of the reconstructed trajectories, not a fitted potential or an estimate of dissipation, and interpreting trajectory loops in terms of dissipation, entropy production or allostatic load would require independent validation. Whether richer dynamics, such as state-dependent noise, time-varying kinetics or coupling between the drives, could be detected from RR intervals alone is an open question that requires a more complex model and an identifiability analysis similar to the one used here.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
Highlights




RR alone may leave vagal-like and sympathetic-like drives ambiguous
A phase-domain state-space model filters irregular RR intervals in continuous time
Physiological priors and a spectral anchor restrict the set of latent solutions
Atropine removes most vagal-like variability; propranolol alone does not
How change is split between the two drives remains conditional on the anchor
Abstract
Heart rate variability (HRV) is widely used to assess cardiac autonomic regulation, but spectral indices cannot separate overlapping vagal and sympathetic contributions and require stationary windows. We propose SPARK (Stochastic Phase-domain Autonomic Reconstruction Kinetics), a state-space model in which fast (vagal-like) and slow (sympathetic-like) latent drives modulate an integrate-and-fire pacemaker. Conditioning on each beat-to-beat (RR) interval yields exact continuous-time Kalman filtering, tracking both drives beat by beat, with uncertainty, without interpolation or windowing. Because RR alone does not determine this decomposition, time-scale priors, a kinetic ordering and a spectral anchor constrain it, reducing multi-start solutions from a median of 23.5 to 1.0 and single-drive collapse from 75% to 4% of fits. We evaluated SPARK on 313 recordings from three cohorts and on public pharmacological-blockade data, where atropine reduced vagal-like variability to 0.16 of saline in 7 volunteers, whereas propranolol did not (1.42). During head-up tilt, the vagal-like state fell and the sympathetic-like state rose in 10 of 10 recordings; in 263 exercise recordings, median recovery times were 42 s (vagal-like) and 341 s (sympathetic-like); and in 40 young and older adults, latent summaries differed by age and were only partly predicted by conventional HRV metrics (median leave-one-out \(R^2\) = 0.42). The fit diagnostics showed residual structure in most recordings; the slow drive also fell under atropine and is defined by its time scale, not sympathetic specificity; and the split between drives depends on the spectral anchor. SPARK is an open-source, beat-resolved tool for autonomic analysis in non-stationary protocols.
Keywords: Heart rate variability; State-space model; Kalman filter; Identifiability; Autonomic nervous system; Integrate-and-fire; Pharmacological blockade

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.1 Conceptual model
SPARK represents the sinoatrial node as an integrate-and-fire pacemaker whose drift is modulated by two latent drives. Between two consecutive beats at times \(t_{k-1}\) and \(t_k\), starting from \(\phi(t_{k-1}) = 0\), the sinoatrial phase \(\phi\) evolves as a drift–diffusion process,
\[
d\phi(t) = \nu(t)\,dt + \sigma_z\,dW(t), \qquad \nu(t) = \nu_0 - x_p(t) + x_s(t), \qquad t \in (t_{k-1}, t_k],
\]
where \(W(t)\) is a standard Wiener process; a beat occurs the first time \(\phi\) reaches a normalized threshold of \(1\) [14], after which \(\phi\) is reset to zero. The drift \(\nu(t)\) is the instantaneous pacing rate (Hz), \(\nu_0\) the baseline rate, \(\sigma_z\) the diffusion coefficient of threshold-level noise, and \(x_p(t)\) and \(x_s(t)\) the parasympathetic-like and sympathetic-like drives (Hz, deviations from their homeostatic baseline), hereafter the vagal and sympathetic drives for brevity. These labels denote model components distinguished by their kinetics and spectral allocation, not measured neural activity.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.2 Latent autonomic dynamics
The drives are independent, mean-reverting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes [24]:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dx_p(t) &= -\kappa_p x_p(t)\,dt + \sigma_p\,dW_p(t),\\
dx_s(t) &= -\kappa_s x_s(t)\,dt + \sigma_s\,dW_s(t),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\kappa_p\) and \(\kappa_s\) are clearance rates (s\(^{-1}\)) with e-folding times \(\tau_p = 1/\kappa_p\) and \(\tau_s = 1/\kappa_s\). The diffusion coefficients are parameterized through the stationary variances, \(\sigma_b = \sqrt{2\kappa_b V_b}\), with \(V_s = \sigma^2_{sys}\) and \(V_p = \lambda_P\,\sigma^2_{sys}\), so that \(\lambda_P = V_p/V_s\) is the relative vagal variance; the global scale \(\sigma^2_{sys}\) leaves the Kalman gain unchanged and is estimated analytically. The state is augmented with the running integrals of the drives, \(dI_p = x_p\,dt\) and \(dI_s = x_s\,dt\), giving \(\tilde{X}(t) = [x_p, x_s, I_p, I_s]^\top\) and \(d\tilde{X} = A\,\tilde{X}\,dt + G\,dW\) with constant matrices \(A\) and \(G\). The transition over any observed interval \(\Delta t_k\) is the matrix exponential \(\Phi_k = \exp(A\,\Delta t_k)\), with a closed-form process covariance (supplementary sections “Matrix exponential” and “Estimation algorithm”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.3 Observation model: phase-domain inversion
Under strict first passage, the interval \(T = \inf\{t > 0 : \phi(t) \ge 1\}\) is inverse Gaussian for a constant drift [15], and a time-varying drift makes the state-space problem nonlinear [7,17]. We instead condition on the observed interval and impose that the phase accumulated over \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) equals one,
\[
1 = \nu_0\,\Delta t_k - \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} x_p(t)\,dt + \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} x_s(t)\,dt + \eta_k ,
\]
where \(\eta_k\) is Gaussian threshold-level noise with variance \(\sigma_z^2\,\Delta t_k\) and \(\sigma_z^2 = \sigma^2_{sys}\lambda_R\). This terminal-threshold condition drops the requirement that \(\phi\) stay below 1 within the interval, which is accurate when the drift is large relative to the noise (an explicit bound is given in the supplementary section “Asymptotic convergence”). In the augmented state the observation is linear,
\[
1 - \nu_0\,\Delta t_k = H\,\tilde{X}_k + \eta_k, \qquad H = [0,\ 0,\ -1,\ 1],
\]
so the Kalman recursions are exact. After each measurement update the integral states are reset to zero while \(x_p\) and \(x_s\) continue to evolve, which represents the restart of phase accumulation at each beat while preserving the memory of the drives across beats. To limit the influence of ectopic beats and detection artifacts, the noise variance at each beat is inflated by a multiplier that grows with the largest relative change between adjacent intervals (supplementary section “Extended methods and discussion”); recordings with substantial non-sinus activity are outside the intended scope.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.4 Model assumptions and identification structure
The physiological information that restricts the admissible solutions is listed in Table 1. These specifications are model assumptions informed by external evidence; they are not estimated from the present data, and their influence is evaluated by the identifiability analyses below.

The ordering \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\) removes label switching, that is, a solution in which the fast and the slow process exchange roles. The time-scale priors reflect rapid vagal and slow sympathetic effector kinetics [2,20,22,28] and are fixed across recordings. The ratio \(\lambda_P\) is a deterministic function of the global wavelet spectrum of heart rate [29,30], partitioned into vagal and sympathetic energy with logistic frequency weights that encode pharmacological-blockade evidence [21–23,31,32]. Because it is computed from the series being fitted, \(\lambda_P\) is data-informed, and equating the ratio of spectral energies with the ratio of latent variances is an approximation (supplementary section “Spectral anchoring”). The jitter prior, which spans the range expected for electrocardiographic and photoplethysmographic acquisition, limits the extent to which the noise term can absorb autonomic variability.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.5 Inference and uncertainty
The Kalman recursion, with the Joseph form of the covariance update, processes the intervals sequentially. The baseline \(\nu_0\) and the scale \(\sigma^2_{sys}\) are profiled out analytically by generalized least squares, using two filters that share one Kalman gain. The remaining parameters \(\theta = (\ln\kappa_s,\ \ln(\kappa_p - \kappa_s),\ \ln\lambda_R)\) are estimated by maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation: the negative profiled log-likelihood plus the negative log-prior terms of Table 1 is minimized with the Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) algorithm from three starting points, keeping the best run. States are then estimated by forward filtering conditional on the recording-level estimates; because parameter estimation and the spectral anchor use the whole recording, the overall procedure is retrospective rather than strictly causal. The state intervals are conditional on the MAP parameters, and standard errors of \(\kappa_p\), \(\kappa_s\) and \(\lambda_R\) come from the numerical Hessian and the delta method (supplementary section “Estimation algorithm”). The model was implemented in R, and a browser implementation with the same specification is available for single recordings (see Code availability).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.6 Model diagnostics
Filtered tracking accuracy is quantified by the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) between the observed and the implied RR; these are in-sample measures, not prediction errors. If the model is adequate, the standardized innovations \(z_k\) are independent standard normal variates, so their probability integral transform \(\Phi(z_k)\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\). This was tested with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) distance \(D\) against the approximate critical value \(1.36/\sqrt{N}\), whose behavior under a correctly specified model was examined by simulation, and serial dependence with the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) of \(z_k\) over 40 lags (supplementary section “Goodness-of-fit diagnostic”).

2.7 Identifiability analyses
Four nested specifications were compared (Table 2). All keep the structural constraints of Table 1, and \(M_3\), which combines all the physiological information, is used in every other analysis. In \(M_0\) and \(M_1\), \(\lambda_P\) is a free parameter; in \(M_2\) and \(M_3\) it is fixed by the spectral anchor.

Each specification was fitted from the same 100 dispersed starting points in a deterministic subset of up to 100 recordings per dataset. For each recording and specification we computed the number of distinct solutions; the near-equivalent fits (profiled log-likelihood within 2 units of the best) and the dispersion of \(\ln\tau_p\), \(\ln\tau_s\) and of the reconstructed trajectories among them; the share of \(x_p\) variance and the proportion of fits in which one process absorbed essentially all variability (share below 0.05 or above 0.95; one-process collapse); the proportion of fits inside the 95% prior intervals; and the fit to RR (definitions in the supplementary section “Identifiability and sensitivity analyses: details”). Because the priors alter the objective, specifications are compared on the profiled log-likelihood and RR error, not on the posterior objective. In addition, profile surfaces of the objective were computed over a \(100 \times 100\) grid of \((\tau_p, \tau_s)\); synthetic series with known drives were fitted in four scenarios (true time scales inside or outside the priors, vagal- or sympathetic-dominant variance); each hyperparameter was varied and each prior component removed in turn; and, to locate the boundary of identifiability, recordings were simulated over the time-scale ratio \(\tau_s/\tau_p\) (with \(\tau_p\) = 4 s), the variance ratio \(\lambda_P\) and the recording length (5, 10 and 30 min) (supplementary section “Identifiability boundary”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.8 Data, preprocessing and event definition
Data and cleaning. RR intervals were derived from the electrocardiogram (ECG; a Polar H10 chest strap in the exercise cohort), with blood pressure, respiration (Fantasia database) or the tilt angle (Physiologic Response to Changes in Posture, PRCP, database) when available; the model itself uses only RR. RR intervals and covariates were cleaned with an adaptive running-median gate, chosen on simulated series with injected artifacts because it altered about 0.2% of artifact-free beats while correcting about 99.7% of artifacts (supplementary section “Data preparation and its checks”).
Participants. The PRCP database contains ten healthy adults, without reported age or sex. The Fantasia database contains 20 young (21–34 years) and 20 older (68–85 years) healthy adults, with equal numbers of women and men in each group as reported by the database. The exercise cohort consists of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older from the Magallanes region of Chile, whose sample is described in the original study [33]; 263 recordings were analyzed, and the recordings carry no subject characteristics. The blockade dataset comprises seven healthy volunteers, six of them men, aged 29.4 ± 2.3 years (mean ± SEM) [34].
Events. Each tilt and stand-up of the PRCP protocol is analyzed against its own baseline. Onsets came from the tilt-angle signal or the protocol annotations and otherwise, as in the exercise recordings, from piecewise-constant segmentation of heart rate; such events are detected from the modeled RR series, so timing relative to them is not independent evidence about the states (supplementary section “Event detection”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.9 Validation framework: orthostatic perturbation
The first biological test uses the PRCP tilt-table recordings [35]. The expected responses are a fast reduction of the vagal drive after tilt onset and a slower, sustained increase of the sympathetic drive; such a test can show that the components behave coherently, not that they are the autonomic branches. Each maneuver was analyzed against its own baseline (60 to 180 s, beginning 120 s after the previous maneuver returned) and a 120-s recovery window. We computed (i) the change in the mean of each state, standardized by its baseline standard deviation (SD); (ii) whether each change had the expected sign; and (iii) a step-response fit, \(x(t) = x_0 + D\,[1 - e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}]\) for \(t \ge t_0\), giving the latency, the time constant and the onset lag \(t_{0,s} - t_{0,p}\). Between-recording summaries used the median over the tilts of each recording. As a negative control, the same contrast was computed between the two halves of each resting baseline (exact 95% intervals; paired signed-rank test of the absolute standardized changes). Secondary analyses (comparison with a continuous wavelet transform, CWT, moving spectrum; the arterial-pressure response; the dose–response over tilt angle; the responses by kind of maneuver) are in the supplementary section “Secondary analyses of the perturbation”.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.10 Generalization: aging
Resting recordings of the Fantasia database [36] were analyzed in a fixed window (600 s starting at 600 s of the recording), with group membership as the only subject characteristic. The latent summaries were \(\nu_0\), \(\tau_p\), \(\tau_s\), \(\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)\), \(\lambda_P\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\), the equivalent timing jitter, the SD of each state, their ratio and the share of \(x_p\) variance. Group differences (older minus young) were summarized by the Hodges–Lehmann shift, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Cliff’s \(\delta\) with a bootstrap interval, with Benjamini–Hochberg control within each family of variables (latent and conventional HRV); with the group sizes available, all tests are exploratory. Stability was assessed by refitting two non-overlapping windows of each recording, with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(3,1)) of the log values. To examine how far the time constants are set by their priors, both windows were also refitted with weak priors (95% intervals 0.5–60 s and 10–2000 s) and with empirical-Bayes priors estimated on the other half of the subjects (supplementary section “Partial pooling of the time constants”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.11 Exercise and recovery
The exercise recordings follow a two-minute step test with a rest–exercise–rest protocol [33]; each is fitted with time-invariant kinetics, so the non-stationary response is carried by the filtered states. The rest level of each state is its mean and SD from 20 s after the start to 5 s before the detected onset; the exercise response is the difference between the mean over the last 15 s of exercise and the rest level; and the path in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane, with the states \(u\) and \(v\) in rest-SD units, is summarized by its length, the area it encloses and its maximum quadratic energy \(E = (u^2 + v^2)/2\), descriptive measures introduced for this representation. Recovery times used the combination of four candidate definitions and three end-of-exercise rules that scored best on simulated recordings with known recovery constants, with right-censoring and Kaplan–Meier medians (supplementary section “Recovery-time benchmark”).
Perturbation-response descriptors. As a complement that uses both states and their uncertainty, we computed the descriptors proposed for latent autonomic trajectories [37]: the largest distance from the resting region during the perturbation, the time after its end from which the state stays within that region for 15 s, the probability of such a return within a horizon, and whether a second-stage hidden Markov model places the end of the horizon in a regime other than rest. Distances are in units of the stationary SDs of \(M_3\) refitted to the resting beats alone, the tolerance is the 0.999 quantile of the stationary distance, and uncertainty comes from paths drawn from the filtered distributions; their recovery was first checked on simulated recordings with known states (supplementary section “Perturbation-response descriptors”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 2.12 Pharmacological blockade and sympathetic nerve activity
text:
2.12 Pharmacological blockade and sympathetic nerve activity
To test the labels of the two drives against an external manipulation, we used a public dataset in which seven healthy volunteers were studied supine with saline, atropine (0.04 mg/kg), atropine followed by propranolol (0.2 mg/kg; double blockade) and, on a second day, propranolol alone, each condition with 5 min of spontaneous and 5 min of 0.25-Hz paced breathing, and with simultaneous ECG and integrated muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) [34,38]. \(M_3\) was fitted, unchanged, to every segment, and the stationary SDs of the two drives under each drug were expressed as ratios to saline of the same day and summarized by their geometric mean with a bootstrap 95% interval over volunteers. The expectations were fixed before the first fit: atropine reduces the SD of the vagal-like drive to less than 0.3 of saline in most volunteers, propranolol alone does not reduce it, and double blockade reduces both drives. In the saline period of each session, \(M_3\) was also fitted across a hyperventilation and a breath-hold, which raises MSNA, and the changes of the states, heart rate and MSNA from the resting baseline were compared (supplementary section “Pharmacological blockade and muscle sympathetic nerve activity”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 2.13 Conventional HRV comparators and statistical reporting
text:
2.13 Conventional HRV comparators and statistical reporting
The SD of RR intervals (SDNN), the root mean square of successive RR differences (RMSSD), mean heart rate, and low-frequency (LF) and high-frequency (HF) power from a tapered periodogram of the resampled tachogram serve as comparators, through rank correlations with the latent summaries and, in the Fantasia recordings, leave-one-out prediction and group discrimination (supplementary section “Additional analyses of the Fantasia recordings”). Quantities that vary across recordings are summarized as the median and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range across recordings, which describes dispersion and is not a confidence interval for the median; proportions carry exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% intervals. None of the analyses was preregistered: those on the PRCP, Fantasia and exercise recordings are exploratory, whereas the expectations of the blockade analysis were fixed before its first fit. Random seeds are fixed throughout.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 3.1 RR alone is insufficient for the latent decomposition
text:
3.1 RR alone is insufficient for the latent decomposition
We first fitted the model without physiological information (\(M_0\)) from dispersed starting values in 150 recordings drawn from the three datasets; under-determination would appear as solutions with comparable fit to RR but different latent decompositions. Without physiological information (\(M_0\); 150 recordings), the multi-start fits of a recording reached a median of 23.5 distinct solutions, with 60.0 fits within 2 log-likelihood units of the best, and one process absorbed essentially all variability in 75% of the fits. Under the full specification (\(M_3\)), the corresponding values were 1.0 distinct solutions, 100.0 near-equivalent fits and one-process absorption in 4% of the fits. The dispersion of \(\ln\tau_s\) among near-equivalent fits under \(M_3\) was lower than that under \(M_0\) (0.00 versus 0.01; larger under \(M_0\) in 3 of 3 datasets: exercise, fantasia and prcp); it was small under both specifications, so the contrast rests mainly on the number of distinct solutions and on one-process solutions. The best RR error under \(M_3\) was higher than that under \(M_0\) (3.39 versus 1.00 ms; a factor of 3.4, small in absolute terms but not in relative terms). In these recordings, the RR series alone therefore left the latent decomposition less well determined than the constrained specification, consistent with the premise that physiological information is needed to restrict the admissible solutions. This shows that the constraints reduce the ambiguity; it does not show that the retained solution is the correct decomposition. The solutions reached from dispersed starting points are shown in Figure 1.

The single solution under \(M_3\) is conditional on the spectral anchor and the priors. (B) Profile of the objective over \((\tau_s, \tau_p)\) for one recording, with the end points of its starts and the prior interval (dashed box); white areas inside the plotted range are grid points without a finite value. Under \(M_3\), 21 of the 100 starts of this recording stopped at a local optimum 191 log-likelihood units below the best fit (outside the contours); the others reached the same optimum. The median SD of \(\ln\tau_s\) among near-equivalent fits was 0.01 for \(M_0\), 0.00 for \(M_1\), 2.83 for \(M_2\), 0.00 for \(M_3\) (lowest under \(M_3\)). One process absorbed essentially all variability in 75% under \(M_0\), 83% under \(M_1\), 23% under \(M_2\) and 4% under \(M_3\) of the fits. Time-scale priors alone (\(M_1\)) therefore did not prevent one-process solutions, whereas the specifications that include the spectral anchor (\(M_2\), \(M_3\)) largely did; the lower ambiguity under \(M_3\) thus comes largely from fixing the variance ratio of the two drives through the anchor, and it should not be read as evidence that the apportionment between the drives is correct. For the vagal-like drive, most estimates therefore lay outside the 95% prior interval, so the data moved \(\tau_p\) away from the central region of its prior; this may reflect slower fluctuations being absorbed by the faster drive, and it limits the reading of \(\tau_p\) as a strictly vagal time constant. In simulations with known truth, when the true time constants lay outside the prior intervals, the median absolute log-error of \(\tau_s\) was 1.32 for \(M_0\) and 0.98 for \(M_3\) (the \(M_3\) error was lower than the \(M_0\) error); when they lay inside, 1.40 and 0.19. These values delimit the claim: constraints that help when the truth is compatible with them can bias the estimates when it is not. The 95% intervals of the filtered \(M_3\) states, which are conditional on the MAP parameters, contained the true state at 70% to 100% of the time points across the four scenarios; the lowest coverage was that of \(x_s\) in the sympathetic-dominant variance scenario (70%).
Simulations from the model itself locate where the decomposition can be recovered (30 recordings per condition; Supplementary Figure S11): with \(M_3\), the correlation between the filtered sympathetic-like state and the truth was 0.38–0.55 when \(\tau_s/\tau_p\) was 4 or less, 0.65–0.68 at 10 and 0.54–0.80 at 30–100 with recordings of 10–30 min. Without physiological information (\(M_0\)), one drive absorbed all the variance in 66% of the fits when the ratio was below 10 and in 17% when it was 10 or more (at least 10 min); with \(M_3\), in 0% and 0%, so the priors prevent the collapse but cannot create identifiability where the time scales overlap. The weaker drive is the one that is lost: with \(\lambda_P\) = 20 the correlation of the sympathetic-like state was 0.25–0.38, and with \(\lambda_P\) = 0.2 that of the vagal-like state was 0.57–0.63.
For \(M_3\), optimization converged for 313 of 313 recordings (100.0%; exercise (n = 263), fantasia (n = 40), prcp (n = 10)). The filtered reconstruction of RR had an in-sample MAPE of 0.222% [0.003, 5.544] and an RMSE of 2.611 ms [0.025, 89.252]. The innovation diagnostics indicated residual serial structure or a departure from the assumed innovation distribution in most recordings (the KS distance was below its critical value in 22% of them): the median KS distance was \(D\) = 0.056 [0.023, 0.177] against a mean critical value of 0.0376, compared with 0% of well-specified simulations exceeding it, and 13.0 PACF lags lay outside the approximate bounds on average (Supplementary Figure S10). This residual structure plausibly reflects respiratory and baroreflex oscillations that the model does not represent, and the states are conditional on it. The e-folding times were 15.05 s [2.61, 44.17] (vagal drive) and 150.0 s [112.6, 220.9] (sympathetic drive), MAP estimates under informative priors and the enforced ordering (supplementary section “Fit and innovation diagnostics”).

3.3 Latent states during orthostatic perturbation
In the PRCP recordings, the tilts were taken from the tilt-angle signal where available (10 of 10 recordings) and from the protocol annotations otherwise; 40 tilts and 20 stand-ups were analyzed. The states of one recording and the average response to a tilt are shown in Figure 2.






Figure 2: Latent states during repeated orthostatic perturbation. (A) One recording (recording 12734, median standardized response): filtered drives (blue, vagal-like \(x_p\); red, sympathetic-like \(x_s\)) with 95% intervals conditional on the MAP parameters, heart rate, mean arterial pressure (ABP) and tilt angle; each tilt is shaded and numbered, and each stand-up (green) is labeled S. (B) All tilts aligned on their onset, each relative to its own baseline (states in baseline SDs; heart rate and ABP as changes); the line is the median over recordings, the band the quartiles and the grey lines the individual recordings. (C) Median path of the two states in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in baseline SDs. (D) Standardized change of the two states between baseline and tilt (large points: recordings; small points: individual tilts); changes of \(x_s\) reach tens of baseline SDs because the baseline SD of \(x_s\) is small. (E) Onset of the response of each state, and of ABP when available, relative to the tilt onset (open symbols: at a search bound). (F) Step-response time constants. (G) Peak lagged correlation between each state and ABP after detrending, with its lag (the sign differs between recordings, so it is not a consistent coupling). When recordings with several tilt-angle levels are available, a further panel shows the mean states, heart rate and ABP by angle. The accuracy of the heart-rate-based events is shown in Supplementary Figure S5.



In 10 recordings with a defined perturbation (40 tilts, each analyzed against its own baseline; a recording contributes the median over its tilts), the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10 (exact 95% interval 69% to 100%), which is consistent with the expected pattern of vagal withdrawal with sympathetic engagement. The same pattern was present in 98% of the individual tilts. As a negative control, the same contrast applied to the two halves of each tilt’s resting baseline gave the expected pattern in 13 of 40 baselines (32%; exact 95% interval 19% to 49%), against 39 of 40 tilts (98%; 87% to 100%), so the pattern is clearly less frequent without a perturbation; the median absolute standardized change was 7.3 times larger for \(x_p\) and 8.2 times larger for \(x_s\) during the tilt (exact paired signed-rank test over 10 recordings, one-sided: \(p < 0.001\) for both). The 25% expected for two independent random signs lies within this interval, so slow drift within the baseline is possible but is not demonstrated. Because heart rate rises during tilt, the net change of the two states is largely fixed by RR; what the spectral anchor and the priors determine is how that change is apportioned between the two drives. The sympathetic-like response began a median of 11.0 s after the vagal-like response, and its time constant was higher than that of the vagal-like response (80.7 versus 3.8 s); 70% of the \(x_p\) and 50% of the \(x_s\) step-response fits reached a search bound, so these constants are approximate. With 10 recordings and with events partly defined from the same RR series, this is a test of physiological coherence and not evidence that the components correspond to the activity of the respective autonomic branches.
Responses by kind of maneuver, the arterial-pressure response and its lagged correlation with the states, the dose–response over tilt angle and the comparison with a CWT moving spectrum are reported in the supplementary material (sections “Secondary analyses of the perturbation” and “Responses by type of maneuver”).

section: 3.4 The latent representation across healthy aging
text:
3.4 The latent representation across healthy aging
Among 20 young and 20 older adults, 8 of 11 latent variables reached \(|\delta| \geq 0.33\): \(\tau_p\) (higher in older adults, \(\delta\) = 0.72; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), \(\lambda_P\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.53; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.71; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), the SD of \(x_p\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.81; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), the SD of \(x_s\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.61; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), the SD ratio \(x_p/x_s\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.54; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), \(\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.69; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)) and the share of \(x_p\) variance (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.54; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)); 2 of 4 HRV variables reached \(|\delta| \geq 0.33\): SDNN (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.71; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)) and RMSSD (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.81; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)). These latent summaries are not independent: the share of \(x_p\) variance is a monotone function of the SD ratio of the two states, both depend strongly on the spectral anchor \(\lambda_P\), \(\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)\) combines the two time constants, and \(\sigma^2_{sys}\) and the SDs of the states scale with the overall amplitude of variability, so that the count above overstates the number of distinct dimensions in which the groups differ. Agreement between two non-overlapping windows of the same recording (ICC of the log values) had a median of 0.88 for the latent summaries and 0.93 for the conventional HRV metrics; the lowest agreement was that of \(\tau_s\) (0.31). With these group sizes, all comparisons are exploratory, and no continuous age, sex or other covariates were available. When the priors of the time constants were replaced by weak ones or by empirical-Bayes priors estimated on the other half of the subjects, the test-retest ICC of the amplitudes stayed at 0.88–0.95, that of \(\tau_p\) was 0.88, 0.54 and 0.70 and that of \(\tau_s\) 0.31, 0.48 and 0.54 (production, weak, empirical Bayes; supplementary material), so the slow time constant carries recording-specific information that the fixed prior suppresses but remains the least reliable summary. Group contrasts are shown in Figure 3 and listed, with the respiration measures, in the supplementary section “Additional analyses of the Fantasia recordings”.

section: 3.5 Latent dynamics during exercise and recovery
text:
3.5 Latent dynamics during exercise and recovery
In the two-minute step-test recordings, the reconstruction tracked the changes in RR across rest, exercise and recovery (Figure 4, panel A). The recovery definition (90% recovery of the excursion) and the end-of-exercise rule (offset time of the fitted exercise profile) were those selected by the simulation benchmark (Supplementary Figure S3).
In 263 of 263 exercise recordings the rest, exercise and recovery phases could be defined from heart rate. From rest to the end of exercise, the vagal-like state changed by -7.9 [-26.9, -1.4] and the sympathetic-like state by 24.9 [5.5, 59.5] rest SDs, with a heart-rate increase of 40 [19, 117] bpm (median [2.5th, 97.5th percentile] across recordings). Recovery times (90% recovery of the excursion; Kaplan-Meier medians) were 42 s for the vagal-like state (1% of recordings censored) and 341 s for the sympathetic-like state (37% of recordings censored). For a first-order relaxation, recovery to 90% of the excursion takes about \(2.3\,\tau\), so these times are of the order implied by the estimated time constants, which are themselves shaped by their priors; they describe the fitted kinetics and are not independent measurements of recovery. The path in the state plane had a median length of 214 [95, 590], an enclosed area of 215 [38, 1051] and a maximum energy \(E\) of 253 [36, 1525] in rest-SD units. In the state plane, the strongest basin of the occupied region (the mode of the density of the filtered states) was displaced from its position in the rest phase by 9.3 rest-SD units to the exercise phase and 2.3 rest-SD units to the recovery phase (Supplementary Figure S6); the number of basins detected was 1 in the rest phase, 3 in the exercise phase, 1 in the recovery phase. The landscape is a descriptive map of where the states lie and is not a fitted potential of the model. Conventional HRV metrics predicted the latent summaries of this cohort with a median leave-one-out \(R^2\) of 0.39. The strongest rank correlation between a latent response and an HRV change was -0.65 (standardized change of the vagal-like state with the change in SDNN, n = 263). No subject characteristics or clinical and functional outcomes were available for this cohort, so the analysis is descriptive and no association with such variables is reported.
Descriptors of the perturbation response computed from the states with their uncertainty, as proposed for latent autonomic trajectories [37], gave a median time to a sustained return to the resting region of 173 s (10th–90th percentile 80–311) after exercise, which correlated with the recovery times above at Spearman 0.72 (\(x_p\)) and 0.63 (\(x_s\)); the probability of return depended mainly on the horizon (0.27, 0.75 and 0.97 at 120, 300 and 600 s), and in simulations the recovery time was recovered in rank but not exactly (Supplementary Figure S12).

(B) All recordings aligned on the end of exercise, each relative to its rest level (median, bands of 25–75% and 10–90% of recordings, and the recording of A). (C) Recovery times of each state (open symbols: right-censored at the end of the recording; bars: Kaplan–Meier medians). (D) Filtered states in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in rest-SD units, one panel per phase on common axes (central 99% of the pooled points): density of the points of the phase (colored hexagons) over that of all phases (grey), ellipses holding 50% (solid) and 90% (dashed) of them, and the median path through the phase (arrow; open circle: start).

text:
3.6 Response to pharmacological blockade
We fitted \(M_3\), unchanged, to 81 five-minute segments of 7 volunteers who received saline, atropine (0.04 mg/kg) and propranolol (0.2 mg/kg). Relative to saline of the same session (geometric mean over volunteers), atropine reduced the standard deviation (SD) of the vagal-like drive to 0.16 (95% CI 0.11–0.21) during spontaneous breathing (below 0.3 in 6 of 6 volunteers) and to 0.18 (95% CI 0.13–0.22) with paced breathing, while heart rate rose by a median of 47 bpm; with propranolol added it fell to 0.10 (95% CI 0.07–0.16). Propranolol alone did not reduce it (ratio 1.42, 95% CI 0.96–2.06; at least 0.8 of saline in 6 of 7 volunteers). The SD of the sympathetic-like drive, however, also fell under atropine, to 0.26 (95% CI 0.16–0.40; by more than a factor of three in 3 of 6 volunteers), and to 0.13 (95% CI 0.08–0.23) under the double blockade: once the vagal part of the spectrum is removed, the spectral anchor re-assigns the variance, so the slow drive is not independent of the fast one in this reconstruction. In the same volunteers the integrated muscle sympathetic nerve signal (MSNA) was higher in the second half of a breath-hold than at baseline in 11 of 14 sessions, but the sympathetic-like state rose in only 3 of 14 (median change -1.3 baseline SDs), and across sessions the change of MSNA correlated with that of \(x_s\) at Spearman -0.17 (\(x_p\) -0.13, heart rate 0.01); during hyperventilation \(x_s\) rose in 14 of 14 sessions, \(x_p\) fell in 13 of 14 and heart rate rose in 14 of 14, and the median lag-0 correlation of \(x_s\) with MSNA over the whole saline period was 0.05. The blockade therefore supports the identity of the fast drive, and the maneuvers show that the slow drive behaves as an acceleratory component of the heart rate, as it is defined, and not as a measure of sympathetic outflow (Figure 5).
