(B) Change from the resting baseline, in baseline SDs, of the integrated muscle sympathetic nerve signal (MSNA), the two states and heart rate in the second half of a breath-hold and during hyperventilation, in the saline period of each session (points: sessions).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.1 Principal observations
We examined whether a physiology-informed state-space model can reconstruct model-conditional autonomic dynamics from RR intervals when the latent decomposition is not identified by RR alone. In the recordings analyzed, adding the physiological information reduced the number of distinct latent solutions and the occurrence of one-process solutions relative to RR alone at a cost in RR error. In the datasets analyzed, the innovation diagnostics indicated residual serial structure or a departure from the assumed innovation distribution in most recordings, so the reconstructions are conditional on a noise model that holds only approximately; with this caveat, in the tilt-table, aging and exercise analyses, the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in most tilt-table recordings; most of the partly redundant latent summaries differed between young and older adults; and the exercise recordings showed a rest-exercise-recovery trajectory whose recovery times are closely tied to the fitted time constants. Beyond these checks of internal consistency, one external test was possible: in a public blockade dataset, the vagal-like drive behaved as a vagal component, whereas the sympathetic-like drive was not independent of it and did not follow sympathetic nerve activity. The representation is therefore best read as a fast drive with pharmacological support and a slow drive defined by its time scale.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 4.2 Physiological meaning and relation to conventional HRV
text:
4.2 Physiological meaning and relation to conventional HRV
The latent trajectories are physiologically constrained reconstructions: they describe the drives that the model needs, given its kinetic and spectral assumptions, to account for the observed interval timing, and this is the sense in which the components are called vagal-like and sympathetic-like. During orthostatic tilt, the reconstructed vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10 recordings (100%), a pattern consistent with the expected autonomic adaptation to orthostatic stress. The same contrast was clearly less frequent in the resting baselines (negative control), where it reflects drift and not a perturbation. The pharmacological data add an external test that the main datasets lack: the vagal-like drive lost most of its variability under atropine (0.16 of saline) and not under propranolol alone (1.42), as a vagal component should, whereas the sympathetic-like drive lost variability under atropine too and did not follow muscle sympathetic nerve activity during breath-holds; the label of the fast drive is therefore supported by blockade, and that of the slow drive remains a statement about its time scale. The path geometry in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane and the quadratic energy \(E\) are descriptive devices, not an energy or a dissipation of the physiological system.
Conventional HRV summarizes how variable RR is; SPARK asks what latent state could account for how RR changes and how that state responds and recovers, so the two are complementary. For signal processing, the representation offers what window-based estimates do not: once the recording-level parameters are fitted, the states are updated at every beat without a stationarity window, irregular sampling is handled exactly, and each state carries an uncertainty interval. Window-based spectral estimates trade temporal against frequency resolution under non-stationarity [5,11]; the comparison with a CWT moving spectrum (supplementary material) depends on the assumptions of the filter and does not establish general superiority. In the Fantasia recordings, HRV metrics predicted the latent summaries with a median leave-one-out \(R^2\) of 0.42, so that a substantial part of their variation was not linearly recoverable from SDNN, RMSSD and mean heart rate. Incomplete prediction from a limited set of HRV metrics does not establish incremental clinical value, which requires independent outcomes.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.3 Identification and physiological priors
In an underdetermined inverse problem, physiological knowledge is part of the identification structure (Table 1), and two consequences follow. First, the kinetic estimates are posterior modes under informative priors that are fixed across recordings: they are regularized toward the priors but not bounded by them, differences in \(\kappa\) between groups should be read together with the prior–posterior contrast, and the separation of fast and slow time scales is built into the structure, not an empirical finding. The boundary simulations show that the priors prevent one-process collapse but cannot create identifiability where the time scales overlap. Second, the spectral anchor assigns branch energy by frequency and is computed from the same recording; conditions in which the two branches overlap in frequency, such as strong orthostatic stress or exercise, may lead to misattribution between the drives [8,39]. The pharmacological evidence on which the spectral weights are based was drawn from the literature. In the one blockade dataset analyzed here, atropine left 0.8% of the RR variance of saline (geometric mean), consistent with reports that at rest vagal blockade removes most of the power at low as well as high frequencies [34]; the weights instead assign most low-frequency variance to the sympathetic branch, which helps explain why the sympathetic-like amplitude fell under vagal blockade and makes the allocation of low-frequency variance the weakest part of the anchor. Varying the physiological hyperparameters one at a time changed the time constants by a median absolute log-ratio of at most 0.64 and left the reconstructed trajectories correlated at least 0.99 with the reference. The direction and time course of the reconstructed states were therefore robust to these settings. Correlations are insensitive to a change of scale, however, and do not address how variance is apportioned between the two drives: the share of latent variance attributed to the vagal-like process changed by a median absolute 0.23 at most, for the vagal floor (0.5), and by 0.37 when the spectral anchor was removed, so statements about the split between the two drives are conditional on the anchor settings (see the limitations).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 4.4 Phase-domain formulation and relation to existing approaches
text:
4.4 Phase-domain formulation and relation to existing approaches
Point-process models of heartbeat intervals based on generalized linear structures are largely phenomenological with respect to the sinoatrial node [15,40], and state-space formulations of integral pulse frequency modulation generally solve the nonlinear first-passage observation in the time domain with extended or unscented filtering [14,17,18]. By conditioning on the observed interval, SPARK obtains a measurement equation that is linear in the integrated drives, together with exact Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transitions across irregular intervals, so the filter is exact and needs no time-stepping approximation; the same structure makes it inexpensive enough to run in a web browser. The price is the terminal-threshold approximation, whose neglected boundary term is bounded in proportion to the ratio of diffusion to the square root of the drift (supplementary material); in the fitted recordings, \(\varepsilon = s_{RR}/\Delta t\) had a median of 0.0063 (maximum 0.0579), corresponding to a bound of at most 0.0116 on the CDF discrepancy. Under strict first passage the interval variance also scales with the inverse cube of the drift, a dependence that SPARK does not represent (supplementary sections “Interval-variance scaling” and “Extended methods and discussion”).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.5 Limitations
The latent states are model-based reconstructions and not measurements of autonomic neural activity; The comparison with pharmacological blockade and with muscle sympathetic nerve activity rests on 7 young volunteers studied supine and at rest in a single public dataset; blockade is not additive and may be incomplete, and it supported only the fast drive: the slow drive lost variability under vagal blockade and did not follow the nerve signal, so it is a slow component of the heart rate and not a measurement of sympathetic outflow. The innovation diagnostics indicated residual serial structure or a departure from the assumed innovation distribution in most recordings (the KS distance was below its critical value in 22% of them), so the reported intervals are conditional on a noise model that holds only approximately. The vagal-like time constant lay inside its 95% prior interval in 19% of recordings, so it should not be read as a strictly vagal time constant: the faster drive may absorb slower fluctuations, such as baroreflex-related oscillations. Recovery times and time constants are shaped by their priors, and in recordings whose duration is comparable to or shorter than the sympathetic time scale, \(\tau_s\) is informed mainly by its prior. The hyperparameters are fixed across recordings, kinetics and variances are constant within a recording, the states are filtered and not smoothed, a better local optimum cannot be excluded for an individual recording, and the simulations use data generated by the model itself. The apportioning of a perturbation-induced change between the two drives depends on the spectral anchor: in the sensitivity analyses the share of latent variance attributed to the vagal-like process changed by a median absolute 0.10 or more with the vagal floor, the spectral crossover and the \(\tau_p\) prior interval. For the same reason the tonic level of each drive is not identified, because \(\nu_0\) and constant offsets of \(x_p\) and \(x_s\) enter the likelihood only through their combination with the mean rate; comparisons of variability, kinetics and mean rate are supported, but not of absolute vagal or sympathetic tone.
The responses by type of maneuver rest on 20 slow tilts, 20 rapid tilts, 20 stand-ups (at most 2 events of a kind per recording) and are descriptive. The tilt-table dataset is small (10 recordings), its tilts are not independent within a recording, and events detected from RR are not independent evidence about the states. Sex and gender were not analyzed: sex is not reported for the PRCP participants or attached to the exercise recordings, six of the seven blockade volunteers were men, and the Fantasia groups are balanced by sex but too small for sex-stratified analyses, so sex differences in the latent dynamics remain untested. The exercise cohort has a single protocol and no clinical outcomes, so the clinical relevance of the trajectories and their behavior in overt autonomic pathology were not evaluated [41,42]. Finally, the single-stream formulation has no respiratory or blood-pressure inputs: respiratory sinus arrhythmia is captured only within the vagal state and baroreflex feedback is implicit [8,43,44], so central autonomic commands cannot be distinguished from peripheral mechanical modulation.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.6 Future directions
Concurrent respiratory and arterial-pressure signals could enter through explicit coupling terms [45–47], reducing reliance on the spectral anchor; larger blockade studies with graded doses and microneurography [48,49] could calibrate the allocation of low-frequency variance; and hierarchical formulations could learn the hyperparameters across recordings. Datasets with clinical outcomes would show whether the trajectories and their perturbation-response descriptors carry prognostic information, and quantities such as the phase-plane geometry or critical slowing down of the kinetics [50,51] could be explored, each requiring dedicated validation.
